 \subsection{The same data, two gold definitions}
-\label{sec:both} The question-level corpus carries two gold generators as well, and this turns out to matter more than the choice between gold definitions. Both definitions leave the measurement undecided, and for a reason that has nothing to do with which definition is used: on 13,104 items each carries a row from each of the two generators, so a disagreement has no strict majority to fall back on. One of those items is not a pair but a quartet: \texttt{customer-service::retention-charged-after-}\allowbreak\texttt{cancel/t0::intent\_pair::}\allowbreak\texttt{intent\_pair} carries two rows from each generator, which is why ``exactly two annotations'' is not literally true of every item and why a row count and an item count part company there. On 12,305 items the two agree and both definitions return that answer; on 799 they disagree, and with two generators a disagreement leaves no strict majority to fall back on. Under our default rule those 799 items leave the gold table, which takes the labelled set to $12,305$ items. The leave-one-out floor is not computed on that set but on the intersection of the two generators' own reduced domains, which the report prints as \texttt{loo\_domain\_size} $=12,406$ items; the two per-generator entries in \texttt{floor\_per\_generator} are \texttt{loo\_n} $=12,903$ and $12,608$, and those are scoring \emph{rows}, not item sets --- they differ from the item counts of the two reduced domains by the duplicated item, so the intersection does not follow from them by subtraction and we do not compute it that way. The leaderboard is scored on the $11,586$ that carry a label inside it, and the tool reports $\mathrm{UNDECIDABLE\_DOMAIN\_MISMATCH}$ for both definitions. Forcing the denominators to agree means resolving every disagreement, and the two definitions then resolve them by different but equally arbitrary rules: majority by sorting the answers as strings, mean probability by comparing the arithmetic mean of the two confidences. The gold definitions then differ, and so do the leaderboards built on them, because each definition also decides which items carry a label at all. Under the forced rule every two-annotation item is labelled, taking the labelled set to $13,104$ and the leaderboard's own scored set to $12,330$, while the floor stays on the same $12,406$-item leave-one-out intersection, so the two terms do not end up on one denominator after all: the instrument returns $\mathrm{UNDECIDABLE\_DOMAIN\_MISMATCH}$ under both definitions. Table~\ref{tab:both} reports the majority leader at $87.91\%$ against a leave-one-out floor of $89.48\%$, a margin of $-1.57$ points with a $95\%$ interval of $[-2.36,\,-0.79]$ that excludes zero. The instrument prints those readings and declines to decide on them. An earlier version of this sentence recorded the corpus as $\mathrm{UNREADABLE}$ under this rule, which is the error this paper exists to describe: a refused comparison is not the negative end of the scale, and a leader sitting below a floor measured on another item set has not been shown to sit below anything. The withdrawal is registered in Appendix~\ref{app:withdrawn}. Neither difference becomes a verdict, because the forced rule is arbitrary and because the two disagree about almost everything above it.
